articles.body: In Brazil, incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is seeking a fourth and final term in the presidential election on October 4. In 2022, he made the fight against hunger and poverty a key campaign promise. Between 2023 and 2024, nearly nine million people were lifted out of poverty thanks to the government’s social and economic programs. The decline was particularly sharp in Brazil’s Northeast. A traditional stronghold for Lula, will the progress made in reducing poverty translate into stronger support for the current president? FRANCE 24's team on the ground reports.
articles.headline: Brazil elections: Can Lula’s anti-poverty record win over voters?

articles.body: The EU said Wednesday it was up to London to chart a way forward for Britain's relations with the bloc, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham put the idea of rejoining on the table. Burnham reopened the divisive Brexit debate Wednesday by saying his centre-left Labour government could go "all the way" and propose membership of the bloc, once it has weighed the "pros and cons" of different possible relationships with Europe. For the European perspective, FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.
articles.headline: Burnham reopens Brexit debate: EU says UK must chart Its own path on future relations

articles.body: Christa Pike, convicted of murdering a schoolmate three decades ago, survived Tennessee's effort to execute her by means of lethal injection late on Wednesday, prison officials said, foiling the state's first attempt to put a woman to death in two centuries. Pike's condition following the ordeal was not immediately known, and it was not clear what legal avenues her lawyers or the state might pursue ​next after she was ‌taken for medical treatment from the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
articles.headline: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt

articles.body: The motive of the Omani copilot who stabbed his captain on a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously and forcing it to land in Saudi Arabia, remained unknown on Thursday as investigators across the region raced to learn more. Our colleagues at France 2 take a closer look at the facts and the unanswered questions, as well as current safety procedures.

articles.body: Republicans know President Donald Trump's unpopularity poses a big problem for them in November. They also recognize he may be their only option to avoid a wipeout. Five weeks before Election Day, many Republicans are facing a damned-if-they-do, damned-if-they-don’t dilemma. Some candidates in close races are wary of alienating undecided voters by campaigning alongside Trump and the baggage that comes with him: High gas prices, voters’ persistent economic concerns and the prolonged war in Iran. But keeping the president at arm’s length could make it harder to turn out the low-propensity base voters they need — voters that only Trump has been able to bring to the polls. “These guys are in a pickle,” said one national GOP operative granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape, like others in this article. “They may not want Trump to come to the district, but there are still things that Trump can do to help.” Asked what would happen if Trump campaigned in a battleground state where their candidates were running, another GOP operative working on midterm races said: “I suspect my candidates would come down with COVID.” But the candidates may not have much of a choice. Trump is increasingly inserting himself into the election in the closing stretch, ramping up his campaign travel with a slate of stops scheduled in red states, repeatedly imploring voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot and, most recently, appearing in taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads that the White House has claimed are Public Service Announcements. Some Republicans have encouraged Trump’s team not to send the president to a blue-leaning Omaha district and other key districts where his approval rating is underwater ahead of Election Day, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. Brinker Harding is running in the Omaha seat being vacated by retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.); his campaign didn’t respond when asked if he’ll attend Trump’s upcoming rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, about a two-hour drive away. Others have said similar things. "They've called me four times now to see if we want him to come, and I've said no," one senior Republican involved in a House GOP battleground race in a district Trump safely won in 2024 told POLITICO. Another Republican operative familiar with Republican midterm strategy said the party views its role — and Trump’s — primarily as driving GOP turnout, while the work of persuading moderates, independents and other swing voters falls more heavily on individual candidates. “Where the president is going is being decided very strategically, to areas where we are trying to boost turnout among Republican voters,” the operative said. “We're not going to be sending him into areas where it would necessarily be hurtful to our candidates.” Others in red states that are increasingly competitive acknowledge that if they want to rally the MAGA base to the degree necessary to hold onto key seats, no one can deliver like Trump. “He's a turnout machine for the Republican Party, the president is,” said Ohio GOP Chair Alex Triantafilou, who will welcome Trump to his state on Saturday. “I certainly know what some of the national polling and some of the pundits have to say about this. But he is always welcome to Ohio because we know that he fires our people up.” Not everyone thinks Trump is a net-positive even in places he comfortably won. A national GOP operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said there are “no indications that there are enough turn out voters to overcome dropping some persuasion voters.” Outgoing North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said he doesn’t think it would be helpful for Trump to campaign in his state — which the president won in all three of his presidential runs, and where former RNC chair Michael Whatley is struggling to tighten the race against former Gov. Roy Cooper. “Not in my opinion — just if you take a look at the votes — you take a look at the independents. I don't think he's the one who's going to get them out,” he told POLITICO. “I think [Trump’s] job is to get the people out who traditionally vote for him and don't show up in off-year elections,” he added. “Our job [as candidates] is to then … create some separation. It's not like you're breaking your loyalty to the president. ... So there are states I think he should go to, there are states I don't think he should go to." The Whatley campaign, however, feels differently. “Who drives R turnout right now in NC — Trump or Tillis? We would welcome Trump back to NC,” said Whatley’s senior adviser, Jonathan Felts. Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have been to North Carolina to campaign with Whatley in recent weeks. Trump’s upcoming stop in a red corner of Ohio outside Dayton is part of a broader campaign swing that reflects the political bind. Other stops scheduled include in deep-red states like Oklahoma and Alabama, as well as in red states with key Senate contests including Ohio, Nebraska and Alaska. Ironically, the expanding battleground map could make Trump more useful to Republicans in some of the places they are most worried about. As the fight has spread into states and districts he won by double digits, simply turning out more of his base may be enough to make a difference. The White House argued Trump is the “unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.” “No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the President understands how to communicate with them,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. The Republican National Committee and National Republican Congressional Committee also said Trump is still a valuable turnout tool, and their candidates are eager to have the president visit their districts and to appear with him on the campaign trail. The National Republican Senatorial Committee did not respond to a request for comment. But some of the voters Republicans most need Trump to activate — especially blue-collar white voters in rural areas who came out to vote for him but often skip voting in the midterms — are themselves unhappy with his presidency. Recent POLITICO polling found that even some of Trump’s strongest supporters — those who identify as MAGA — are souring on his handling of key issues. A POLITICO Poll in August found that a 44% plurality of MAGA Trump voters said the Iran war has made things more expensive for them, while 38% said the war has had no real impact on their costs. “It's really Trump's voting base that's feeling the pain of Trump the most,” said another Republican operative involved in several battleground races across the country, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape.“They have to turn those people out. But those people are pissed at Trump, so it's this weird dynamic of like: ‘Does he help? Does he hurt? Can he go and encourage the disenfranchised, the really pissed off Republican Trump voter?’” the operative said. “That's really going to be what decides the outcome of this election.” It’s noteworthy which GOP candidates are enthusiastically coming out to Trump’s rallies — and which are sitting out or staying mum on their plans. A spokesperson confirmed that Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who is locked in a tough race in a state Trump won by double-digits, will attend Trump’s upcoming rally outside of Dayton; a spokesperson for Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP gubernatorial candidate, did not respond to an inquiry about Ramaswamy’s attendance plans, nor did spokespeople for the trio of GOP House candidates running in Ohio’s competitive 1st, 7th and 9th Districts. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP Senate candidate in Iowa, recently said the Iran war needs to be “ brought to a successful and immediate end ,” in a rare public break with Trump. Hinson also did not attend a campaign rally Vice President JD Vance held in western Iowa in mid-September . She did, however, appear in the Oval Office behind Trump earlier this week when he announced a plan to build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa.   But with an ever-darkening environment, some Republicans see any efforts to reverse course as better than nothing. “Everybody sees the polling,” said Daniel Garza, a Texas Republican strategist and president of the conservative LIBRE Initiative . “Is the polling accurate? I have no idea. All I know is that turnout is going to be key to this, and anything helps right now, at this point.” Jordain Carney and Lisa Kashinsky contributed.
articles.headline: Republicans need Trump to turn out the base. Some candidates still don’t want him.

articles.body: The Supreme Court blocked President Donald Trump’s effort to restrict mail voting. But for Democrats trying to turn out voters, the uncertainty seems harder to put to rest. Fewer Democrats say they plan to vote by mail in November’s midterms than at the same point in 2024, according to a new NBC News poll , as a separate survey finds declining confidence that the Postal Service will deliver election mail on time. That represents an about-face for a party that has increasingly embraced mail voting since the 2020 pandemic election, forcing Democratic strategists to rethink how they get voters to the polls — and how to convince them their ballots will count. Quentin James, founder and president of the Collective PAC, said his group is hearing concerns from Black voters about whether their mailed ballots will be secure and counted. “I think there's confusion,” James said. “We know that the president has spent six months talking about changing the rules regarding mail-in voting, and a lot of folks are concerned about their ballot being secure.” That confusion comes as Democrats and voting groups weigh how to reassure voters after Trump’s latest effort to restrict mail voting. The president signed an executive order in March seeking to crack down on mail-in voting, citing unproven claims that the process is insecure and vulnerable to electoral fraud. “The cheating on mail-in voting is legendary. It’s horrible what’s gone on,” Trump said during an Oval Office signing ceremony. “I think this will help a lot with elections.” Still, the rules for mail ballots — at least nationally — will be effectively the same as 2024 after the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to enforce the new mail-in ballot delivery regulations in a ruling earlier this month . The high court left in place a lower-court decision that blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing the new proposed requirements in the weeks before the midterm election. Despite that, Democratic voters have signaled they are changing how they’ll vote. In the NBC poll, 23% of registered Democrats said they plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in September 2024. Thirty-six percent said they plan to vote early in person, up from 30%, while another 36% expect to vote on Election Day. A Marist poll found that 58% of registered voters were confident the Postal Service would deliver election-related mail to voters and election officials on time, down from 71% in October 2024. Marist also found that Democrats remain more likely than Republicans to plan to vote by mail or absentee ballot, 32% to 12%, respectively. James said his organization has long encouraged early in-person voting through its Rides to Vote program, which provides transportation to voters without a vehicle. But despite the Supreme Court ruling, his organization is also encouraging people considering voting by mail to use a ride voucher to return their completed ballots directly to the required location. “The bigger threat is confusion and fear,” he said. “That is the thing that a court case will not solve, and that's what we're really concerned about.” In Maine, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said municipal clerks have reported voters canceling absentee ballot requests, including requests to receive ballots automatically in future elections. Bellows cautioned against a blanket message to vote in person. “We would discourage advocates from telling people not to vote by mail if, for those voters, that’s their only option,” said Bellows, a Democrat who ran this cycle for governor and in the rapid-fire Senate primary, pointing to older and disabled Mainers who rely on absentee voting. Her office is instead urging voters to make a plan that works for them, return mailed ballots early and use Maine’s online absentee ballot tracking system to check whether a clerk has received and accepted them. “Our public education efforts have been focused on encouraging voters to make a plan that's right for them, and recognizing that they have the peace of mind of tracking their absentee ballot and the backup option of voting on Election Day if, for any reason, the ballot is delayed by the mail,” Bellows said. Indivisible, one of the party’s largest grassroots groups, is mounting its own early-vote push and nudging people to cast their ballots early, regardless of how they vote. Co-founder Leah Greenberg said that the group is helping organize an Oct. 17 national day of action to encourage people to vote early under their states’ rules. “So we were absolutely hearing concern,” Greenberg said. “But more importantly, what we're hearing is people trying to figure out what they can do and how they can organize locally in order to protect elections.” Greenberg said Indivisible is urging voters to get their ballots in early and emphasizing that a court rejected the administration’s attempt to restrict mail voting. Still, the ruling hasn’t erased the uncertainty organizers say they are hearing from voters. Greenberg and James described a similar mix of relief and concern among voters. “People are glad to hear it, but still wary,” Greenberg said. Democrats, including state election officials who oversee the process, are also looking for ways to boost confidence in the mail system. Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar has asked his state’s congressional delegation to arrange election observers at postal facilities handling Nevada’s ballots. In letters to the state’s congressional delegation, Aguilar identified sites in Las Vegas and Reno, as well as facilities in West Sacramento, California, and Salt Lake City, Utah. Aguilar said nearly 670,000 Nevadans voted by mail in 2024 and argued that having observers present could strengthen confidence in ballot handling. In an interview, he said observers would also signal to postal workers that they have support in the process. “By having observers there, it gives them the support to say: ‘Hey, we got your back,’” Aguilar said. “We also want to be helpful if there are any concerns — we want to make sure that leadership knows we are not going to stay quiet. We're going to be proactive. We're going to be engaged and we're going to hold them accountable when we need to hold them accountable.” Aguilar said Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) has requested observers following his letters. Lee’s office did not respond to a request for comment. USPS said it had received correspondence regarding Aguilar’s request and was reviewing it. “The Postal Service has successfully delivered America’s election mail, and we are confident that we will do so again this year,” Nikolaj Hagen, a Postal Service spokesperson, said. Hagen pointed to USPS figures showing it delivered 233.3 million pieces of election mail through Aug. 28 in fiscal year 2026, with 97.94% arriving on time. In the 2022 election, USPS handled 105.4 million ballots and delivered 99.93% of those sent by voters to election officials within seven days. In 2024, it handled 222.39 million pieces of ballot mail , with 99.88% delivered to officials within seven days. Meanwhile, Bellows said Maine is taking a different approach. Local USPS representatives have proposed weekly meetings with her election staff, she said, and her office has relationships with workers at the state’s two distribution centers. But she noted congressional observers could be useful in larger states where those relationships are less established. “Maine is a small enough place where, if there were a problem, we would probably know very quickly through union representatives or simply word of mouth,” Bellows said, noting that congressional observers at postal locations could be particularly useful in places “where those relationships may not be as strong or well established.”
articles.headline: Democrats’ mail-voting plans shift as officials work to reassure voters

articles.body: Sen. Jon Ossoff hosted a few hundred donors and supporters for a recent Washington fundraiser — but it wasn’t just for him. Instead, the Sept. 16 gathering was geared toward raising money for the Democratic Party of Georgia and its coordinated campaign, according to an Ossoff aide and one attendee, who was granted anonymity to describe a private event. It's part of his broader effort to boost state Democrats as they look to flip the governor’s mansion for the first time in over 20 years and improve their margins in the Legislature. And the timing, just weeks before November, signals confidence in Ossoff’s own reelection prospects and the sizable war chest he’s raised for himself . This month’s event was the latest of several similar fundraisers Ossoff has held over the last two years. He plans to host more fundraisers for Georgia’s Democratic Party and the coordinated campaign ahead of Election Day, according to one person familiar with his planning, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. If his moves are successful and November ushers in historic wins for Georgia Democrats, Ossoff will have cemented his status as a serious leader in the critical swing state. He would hold on to a crucial seat in the Senate as the party looks toward the South to shore up its future. He’d be credited in part with helping elect former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the country’s first Black woman governor. And though Ossoff has said he’s not interested in joining a 2028 presidential race, leading a November sweep would ultimately raise his national profile. “It would be hard to call him anything but a leader of the [state] party at that point. He's already inching his way towards that kind of designation,” said Andrew Heaton, a Georgia-based Democratic strategist who supports the ticket. “But if there is the kind of success that a lot of people are predicting for the cycle, he would receive a large portion of the credit for that.” Ossoff’s campaign did not comment beyond confirming the fundraisers. The events are just part of Ossoff’s endeavor to help build out the Georgia Democratic Party’s apparatus after a rough 2024 election cycle. The senator has transferred $3.6 million of his own campaign funds to the party’s coordinated campaign to date, which the Atlanta Journal-Constitution first reported . Since the effort was announced in July, the party has opened 30 field offices across the sizable state and employs more than 100 field staffers helping with grassroots organizing for races up and down the ballot. The coordinated campaign is led by a former Ossoff political director, Kyle Tromley. Caroline Saudek, a longtime fundraiser for Ossoff’s political operation, also joined the state party in January in a fundraising-focused role. Democrats across the state — from the densely populated Atlanta metro to Georgia’s small sliver of Atlantic coast — said they’ve seen a marked difference in the coordinated campaign’s involvement this cycle, from consistent communication to investment in smaller-profile races. That transformation, several noted, started when Chair Charlie Bailey took the helm. Bailey, an attorney from rural Harris County and former statewide candidate for lieutenant governor, became the leader of the party in mid-2025 with Ossoff’s crucial support . “It is definitely a stronger coordinated campaign than I've seen in years, and in previous cycles. And it feels like it is better staffed, they staffed up earlier,” said Heaton, the Georgia-based Democratic strategist. Republicans are also taking note of the newly improved Democratic machine in a state that, until 2020, was a safe-red hold for the most high-profile races. Already, GOP fears are growing about Rep. Mike Collins’ ability to beat Ossoff . And polls show GOP gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson locked in a tight battle with Bottoms, despite having dropped tens of millions from his own bank account into the race. Georgia Republican Party Chair Josh McKoon shrugged off Democrats’ fundraising efforts and said he feels “very good” about Republicans’ field resources. “We've had a field program in place for months now. We have field staff on the ground all over the state,” he said in an interview, though he declined to provide details on the size of the Georgia GOP’s paid and volunteer operation. Others aren’t as dismissive. “The Democratic Party has deployed resources to hire staff that mobilizes and turns out voters. Republicans have not had this competitive of a race in a while, so they don’t have that type of muscle memory,” said Ryan Mahoney, a longtime Georgia-based Republican strategist. “The Democrats are in such a great spot,” he added. “It's because the apparatus has been tested and is working.”
articles.headline: Jon Ossoff is fundraising for Georgia Democrats. It’s a bet for his party’s future — and his own.

articles.body: Facing his toughest election challenge in years, GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has blanketed southeast Pennsylvania with attacks on his Democratic opponent — many of them citing what appear to be independent local news reports. “Bob Harvie calls himself a king,” reads one article quoted in a June television spot . “Bob Harvie has his FBI files but refuses to release them,” reads another headline quoted in a September digital ad . Another quotes , “Bob Harvie to independent voters: ‘join a political party or lose your right to vote.’” These ads and five others all cite headlines from Patch, a “hyperlocal” news organization that has garnered hefty audiences in some communities. Patch employs full-time journalists but also allows locals to post unedited “articles.” That isn’t the only reason to question the reliability of coverage referenced in the ads: Each of the articles cited carry the byline of Dave Sommers, a Levittown, Pennsylvania, man with close ties to Fitzpatrick and a checkered history with law enforcement. The battle for the 1st District has grown increasingly nasty as the five-term incumbent battles national headwinds for Republicans and tries to fend off a spirited challenge from Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner. Central to the GOP defense strategy has been a costly ad blitz, with Fitzpatrick and allies trying to paint Harvie not as a devoted public servant but as an ethically compromised political operator — using Sommers’ headlines as key fodder. Sommers has received sporadic payments and reimbursements from Fitzpatrick’s campaign, as well as from the campaign of his late brother, Republican Rep. Mike Fitzpatrick, dating back to 2010. As recently as 2022, Brian Fitzpatrick’s campaign paid Sommers $500 for “office setup services,” according to Federal Election Commission records. That year, Sommers was charged with stealing an election sign that expressed support for a GOP primary challenger, Alex Entin, according to a local news report . Sommers has been pictured with Fitzpatrick at campaign and personal events. Fitzpatrick’s Facebook page shows Sommers posing next to the lawmaker at a March 2025 St. Patrick's Day parade. Sommers' own Facebook account has featured a stream of posts supporting Fitzpatrick, including one post from June where Sommers is seen sporting a tank top with the phrase “Team Fitz.” Sommers also attended Fitzpatrick's June wedding, according to multiple social media posts. In one wedding photo posted to Sommers’ Facebook , he poses with former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.), also a guest. Sommers did not respond to repeated requests for comment about his relationship to Fitzpatrick and his campaign. Spokespeople for the Fitzpatrick campaign also did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Reilly Richardson, a spokesperson for the House GOP campaign arm, pointed in a statement to a Friday report that Harvie passed off “known Democrat activists” as “concerned voters” in his own ads and accused him of “lying to voters.” “Now, he’s desperately trying to distract from his pathetic, flailing campaign, but Pennsylvanians won’t be fooled,” Richardson said of Harvie. Sommers is a retired reporter who worked for the Bucks County Courier Times, The Trentonian and other local outlets. He drew headlines of his own after he was prosecuted for trafficking in protected turtles . Prosecutors alleged he made more than $500,000 over six years selling diamondback terrapins online, running afoul of state and federal conservation laws . Sommers was handed a six-month prison sentence in 2019, along with six months of house arrest and a $250,000 fine. Sommers opened a more recent chapter as a Patch contributor, posting eight articles dating back to late February. They all attack Harvie, slamming him for being “divisive,” “arrogant” and a “hack.” They feature messaging consistent with the Fitzpatrick campaign, including an Aug. 27 post that accuses Harvie of wanting “more data centers in Bucks County.” Harvie in a statement called Fitzpatrick “a complete and total fraud” and said he’s growing “desperate.” “Brian Fitzpatrick is worse than the rest of the Washington swamp because he pretends to be different, but the receipts show he is corrupt to the core,” he said. Harvie has also repeatedly denied several of the Fitzpatrick campaign and its allies’ characterizations of his record, particularly that he was the target of any FBI investigation. Harvie testified before a federal grand jury with other officials in September 2022 as part of an apparent public corruption probe, according to a local report . He sent a cease-and-desist letter to Fitzpatrick in July, claiming defamation in campaign ads. He also sued the pro-Fitzpatrick Defending America PAC in August for defamatory statements. The use of headlines mined from self-publishing platforms in political ads is not unheard of, with outlets such as Medium and Substack offering opportunities for both parties to pass off politically motivated attacks as independent reporting. Campaigns around the country have drawn scrutiny for leaning on articles in their campaign materials from partisan sources or that misrepresent their origin — but rarely are they citing sources that have such direct ties to the candidate. Posting on Patch, like those other platforms, requires only creating an account. An email associated with Sommers appears to be tied to a Patch account, prompting a “Welcome back!” message when it is used to try to open a new account. CLARIFICATION: This article has been updated to more precisely describe Patch's journalism.
articles.headline: The source of Brian Fitzpatrick’s campaign ad attack fodder: A guest at his own wedding

articles.body: POLICING PROBLEMS: In the early days of his administration, Mayor Zohran Mamdani placed a new requirement on the NYPD: The department would have to secure permission from his office to deploy its Strategic Response Group to make arrests at protests. The directive, which hasn’t been previously reported, shows Mamdani sought to exert significant influence over a core function of the police department. Its existence also calls into question why the mayor hasn’t more frequently used that authority to stop the SRG from being deployed at protests — since he promised as a candidate to disband the specialized unit. The unit — which has long weathered criticism for its heavy-handed protest responses — just last week arrested activists protesting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s appearance at the United Nations General Assembly. Several politicians allied with Mamdani were among those put in handcuffs. When asked about those arrests, an NYPD spokesperson revealed the pre-approval policy to Playbook, confirming that the mayor’s office has the final say whenever the department wants to deploy SRG to detain protesters. “We communicate with City Hall on this topic as we do on a host of things related to the department,” the spokesperson said. The police spokesperson declined to comment on when exactly the mayor first instituted the SRG pre-clearance process. But a person familiar with the timing, who was granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive issue, said the policy was put in place during the first few months of Mamdani’s term. The mayor suggested at a press conference on Monday that he didn’t see a justification for using the SRG in last week’s arrests outside the U.N. “I’ve been clear that my vision is for the disbanding of the SRG,” he told reporters when asked if he thought it was an appropriate use of police resources. A Mamdani spokesperson declined to comment Tuesday on why the mayor didn’t use his power to call back the SRG last week if he didn’t think its deployment was justified. The spokesperson also would not say if the mayor has ever used his authority to reject a request from the NYPD for SRG intervention. Amanda Jack, The Legal Aid Society’s policy director for criminal law reform, laced into the Mamdani administration after being informed of the existing policy. "It is deeply troubling that City Hall has the authority to stop SRG deployments, yet continues to approve them at demonstrations, including at the protests outside the United Nations last week where the mayor himself acknowledged that the deployment was an inappropriate use of police resources,” said Jack, whose group has long advocated for abolishing the SRG. “This further confirms that regulating SRG deployments isn’t the solution. City Hall must finally make good on Mayor Mamdani’s campaign promise to disband SRG for good." The future of the SRG is one of several sources of friction between Mamdani and Jessica Tisch, his politically moderate NYPD commissioner. It’s also an issue that the mayor risks disillusioning his leftist base with the longer he keeps dragging his feet on fulfilling his 2025 campaign pledge. Tisch has defended using the unit, saying it’s a key tool in the department’s network of crime-fighting strategies. But Mamdani — a democratic socialist who, before launching his 2025 mayoral bid, supported calls to defund the NYPD — has long said the unit should be dismantled. Since taking office, he’s said he’s in active conversations with Tisch about finding a way to break up the unit, but those talks haven’t resulted in any tangible action nine months into his term. Founded in 2015, the SRG was initially just tasked with counterterrorism work. The group’s responsibilities have since come to include responding to protests that turn chaotic or violent. In arguing for abolishing the unit, Mamdani and other police reform advocates have pointed to SRG officers racking up disproportionately high rates of misconduct claims while responding to protests. The SRG was subject to a court settlement in 2023 that put new guardrails around how the unit could be deployed during protests. But Mamdani and like-minded voices have contended that’s not enough and that the SRG should be broken up so it can return squarely to its original counterterrorism function. In his remarks on Monday, Mamdani reaffirmed that view. “I have made that promise, I will fulfill that promise,” he said. “The only question is the timeline of it.” — Chris Sommerfeldt  MARK YOUR CALENDAR: Join POLITICO’s New York Outlook: Affordability, Industry & The Economy on Oct. 14 for live conversations about the business and policy decisions being made today — from City Hall to the State Capitol — that will shape the city’s economic future. The lineup includes New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, New York City Economic Development Corp. CEO Anthony Shorris, Partnership for NYC CEO Steven Fulop, Citizens Budget Commission President Andrew Rein, Charles H. Revson Foundation President Maria Torres-Springer, and more. Register now to attend in person or watch the livestream . From the Capitol CORNELL UNDER FIRE: Gov. Kathy Hochul is calling for an independent review of Cornell University’s response to a 2024 gang rape case, as the case draws national attention and the school faces mounting criticism. The Tompkins County district attorney said his office is reopening a criminal probe into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell fraternity house, following a civil lawsuit filed by the plaintiff in mid-September. The plaintiff, a former Cornell student referred to as Jane Doe, alleges in the lawsuit that several men raped her at the Chi Phi house after she was coerced into consuming drugs. The lawsuit names Cornell, several Chi Phi organizations, the former president of Cornell’s Chi Phi chapter, a local bar and unnamed individuals as defendants. The governor called for outside counsel to conduct a “transparent, independent” review of the university’s response to determine whether Cornell “met every obligation to protect its students and pursue justice.” “I support the district attorney’s decision to reopen the criminal investigation,” she said in a statement. “But there are also serious questions about Cornell’s campus culture and its systems for prevention, reporting, and response.” She called the allegations in the case “nothing short of horrifying.” “For any student to come forward after an experience like this takes extraordinary courage,” Hochul said. “No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act.” Rebecca Valli, a Cornell spokesperson, told Playbook the school plans to work with the governor and other state officials. “Cornell shares Governor Hochul’s commitment to addressing campus culture issues, which affect universities across the nation and New York,” Valli said in a statement. “We are committed to continuing to work with state officials to advance student safety and wellbeing.” — Madina Touré EYES ON AI: When it comes to who’s getting involved in addressing the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, Hochul offered a straightforward perspective today: the more the merrier. Speaking to reporters after a meeting of her FutureWorks Commission , which is set to deliver recommendations by the end of the year regarding AI and the workforce, Hochul welcomed the City Council’s recently announced moves to regulate AI . “This is an area where we need an all-hands-on-deck approach,” she said in response to a question regarding whether the Council’s proposals might overlap with the state’s. “I applaud the City Council for getting more information. … If they come up with an idea that would make sense at the state level, we'll embrace it. We have an idea at the state level, it already covers the city. So this is an area, we're on the same team in terms of making sure we get this right, because the risks are too high.” Hochul said the commission is looking to address how AI is reshaping jobs, the best ways to train workers on the technology, protecting those vulnerable to job cuts and “the best ways to harness the benefits of AI for everyday New Yorkers.” Tom Perez, the co-chair of the commission and former U.S. secretary of labor, said there are “more questions than answers at this point” but he has “great optimism that we can tackle this challenge.” — Madison Fernandez FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL SUPER PAC SURGE: Super PACs backing Hochul have reported $4.8 million in contributions since yesterday, giving the governor a comfortable advantage over Republican Bruce Blakeman in the outside spending arms race. Greater Empire State, a committee run by the Democratic Governors Association, received $1 million from the Greater New York Hospital Association – a perennial top spender in New York politics that gave the state Democratic Committee $1.5 million in June. The DGA group also received $500,000 from former gas company CEO John Hess. It reported a dozen four- or five-figure donations from pediatricians and other healthcare groups as well. At least 10 of those have connections to the physician network Somos Community Care, a longtime Hochul benefactor . Additionally, the landlord-backed New York Apartment Association gave $3 million to Leadership for New York, a pro-Hochul super PAC launched by former NYAA official Jay Martin. That committee subsequently transferred $1 million of its money to the one run by DGA. — Bill Mahoney BROOKLYN BATTLE: The state Supreme Court’s appellate division ruled in favor of a group of self-described reformers who were looking to unseat Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn as chair of the Brooklyn Democratic Party. The decision comes just hours before the executive committee is scheduled to meet to vote on the next party chair. Julio Peña III, the district leader put forth by reformers to unseat Bichotte Hermelyn, has been locked in a legal battle over Bichotte Hermelyn’s move to change the makeup of the executive committee — a maneuver she claimed would promote inclusivity, but one her opponents insisted was only carried out to pad her support before the leadership election. A state Supreme Court judge ruled that the vote on the expansion was invalid, but Bichotte Hermelyn appealed the decision. Today’s appellate division ruling voids the expansion — seemingly a win for Peña, who has said he has enough support to win the leadership election under the unchanged structure. But there’s still plenty up in the air. Last night, Bichotte Hermelyn said she decided not to run for another term as chair. After her announcement, City & State reported that she is backing state Assemblymember Nikki Lucas, who had not been actively running for the position. Reformers are in court today looking to prevent this evening’s meeting from happening in light of last week’s chaotic organizational meeting . — Madison Fernandez FROM CITY HALL COMBAT READY: Mamdani released a highly anticipated blueprint to combat rising antisemitism today amid ongoing criticisms that he’s fueled the problem. Under his plan, the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism will weigh in on $26 million that was allocated in this year’s budget to the Mayor’s Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes, which has a broader mandate to fight all forms of hate. The cash infusion will mean more money for organizations already engaged in combating antisemitism online and for supporting victims of antisemitic incidents. In particular, the city has doubled the investment in groups doing this work to $6.4 million and has earmarked $1 million for physical security at sensitive sites like synagogues. And it will work to increase visits to the Museum of Jewish Heritage for middle schoolers. “We hold a responsibility to sustain and protect our Jewish neighbors — a responsibility that belongs to each of us,” Mamdani said in a video message accompanying the report. “That is the work we are undertaking at City Hall, and I am asking every New Yorker to join us.” While the report generated plaudits from across the political spectrum, several prominent Jewish organizations said the mayor failed to define antisemitism and to acknowledge that some of his own rhetoric is to blame. “While the Mayor's plan has a number of positive elements, including some increased security funding for Jewish institutions and expanding proven programs, it fails to address a central issue that the Mayor himself has perpetuated: rhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers,” the UJA-Federation of New York, JCRC-NY, AJC New York and New York Board of Rabbis wrote in a joint statement. Read more from POLITICO’s Joe Anuta here.  BRIDGE TO HOME: NYC Health + Hospitals is opening a second site for the "Bridge to Home" program, an initiative by former Mayor Eric Adams to provide a place for homeless patients to continue healing after a hospital stay. Patients will be able to stay as long as 12 months at the new Crown Heights site in Brooklyn, where they will have 24/7 medical support from Woodhull Hospital providers and get help applying for permanent housing. "Bridge to Home is a bridge between getting well in the hospital and building a life in the community,” Omar Fattal, NYC Health + Hospitals’ chief behavioral health officer, said during a press conference this afternoon. “And for someone like me who spent many years working in inpatient psychiatry, it means that when we ask, 'Where does this person go next?', we finally have a better answer.” Since the first "Bridge to Home" site opened in Midtown Manhattan in September 2025, 18 participants have moved into permanent housing, according to NYC Health + Hospitals. The first resident of the Crown Heights site, which has capacity for roughly 50 program participants, moves in next week. — Maya Kaufman IN OTHER NEWS INFLUENCER ARMY: A group of influencers under instruction from City Hall are reportedly planning a campaign against top New York CEOs, a claim Mamdani’s administration denies. ( New York Post ) ENERGY FUTURE: A flurry of new energy-intensive projects are underway in upstate New York. ( Times Union ) FRUIT FUMES: Bureaucracy and politics have led to the unraveling of a years-in-the-works plan to modernize a diesel-spewing produce market in the South Bronx. ( Gothamist ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .

articles.body: A slate of Democrats are running for Congress leaning on their Christian bona fides. Republicans are trying to portray them as wolves in sheep’s clothing. In Texas, Republicans are running ads blasting seminarian James Talarico for saying he’s “a Christian who hates Christianity.” In Iowa, they are going after a pair of clergy in key House races as “PINOS” — “pastors in name only,” because they “don’t profess the true gospel of Jesus Christ.” In Kansas, Republicans pan megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton as “too woke and too weak.” “His sermons are essentially a carbon copy of the Democrat National Committee platform,” said Brent Robertson, chief of staff to Hamilton’s opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), pointing to a past sermon in which Hamilton urged followers to reduce their carbon footprint . The closing arguments on these Democrats — as evidenced by the most recent ads — shows a concerted effort to turn their preaching against them to paint them as fake, corrupt or even blasphemous . In Texas, MAGA Inc. is on air painting Talarico as a “liberal weirdo,” clipping Talarico’s controversial statements, like “Jesus Christ Himself was a radical feminist” and “God is non-binary.” The Trump-aligned No Going Back PAC is on air in Iowa’s 2nd District hitting Presbyterian minister and Democrat Lindsay James as inauthentic: “When the cameras are on, Lindsay James goes into a character, a caring pastor who says what you want to hear, but when there's no spotlight, Lindsay James shows just how radical she can be.” And in Kansas, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall’s campaign is on air slamming Hamilton as a “slimy,” “millionaire megachurch CEO,” saying he “used faith to fatten his wallet” and “asked churchgoers to pony up for God, then use church resources for his own campaign.” “The swamp's got enough money changers,” the ad says. The attacks are coming precisely because these candidates have proven to be formidable candidates in purple to red areas, using their faith backgrounds to bolster themselves against GOP accusations that they’re out of their state’s mainstream. Talarico poses Democrats’ best chance to flip a Texas Senate seat in nearly four decades. Hamilton has turned deep-red Kansas into a battleground. And James and Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister, are running tough in a pair of Iowa districts Trump won in 2024. Voters “understand and appreciate authenticity, and they know that faith without works is dead,” said Chaz Molder, the Democratic nominee in Tennessee’s deep-red 2nd District who leads a Sunday School class with his wife. “And just posting scripture on Sunday morning to point out that they went to church is not enough.” But with Democrats’ clerical credibility comes a practical challenge: years and years of on-camera sermons, a treasure trove for oppo researchers. It’s become a challenge in Hamilton’s race, where Vice President JD Vance joined the pile-on earlier this month: During a visit to Iowa, he took a shot at Hamilton as having “kind of a ‘gee whiz, I'm a nice pastor’ vibe,” but said he “tells his congregation not about the gospel of Jesus Christ, but that they need to repent for their white privilege while eating beef.” Democrats have largely brushed off the attacks. Talarico has said he’s “missed the mark” on some of his “cringey” past comments but has doubled down on his sermonizing: “When I take on the politicians who are serving themselves and not the people, I’m doing it on biblical grounds,” he said in a sermon last weekend. A James spokesperson criticized Republicans for “desperately attacking Lindsay’s deeply held faith commitments. If it wasn’t so insulting to other Iowa Christians, it would be laughable.” Hamilton has seen clergy run to his side: 120 fellow Methodist ministers across Kansas wrote an open letter to Marshall telling him to stop attacking Hamilton’s pastoral ministry, saying the attacks “tear at the fabric that is the body of Christ.” “We're not the first Christians to be attacked for our faith, and we won't let smears and lies from a couple of Washington politicians stop us from living out our values in the world,” Hamilton said in a video after Vance’s speech. In many ways, this election marks something of a faith resurgence for the Democratic Party. While only half of Democrat- and Democrat-leaning U.S. adults identify as Christian (a 24-percentage-point decline since 2007), Democrats this cycle are running clergy, Sunday School teachers, chaplains and other devout Christians across the map. “As a person of faith, I think that it's time for the Democratic Party to reassert that Democrats are a big tent, and we have many elected officials from different faiths for whom faith is something very important to them,” said Ben McAdams, the Democratic nominee in Utah’s 1st District and a volunteer Sunday School teacher in his Latter-day Saint congregation in Salt Lake City. “The Republican Party of Donald Trump does not seem to be reflecting the Christian values that I grew up with.” Doug Pagitt, executive director of progressive group Vote Common Good, counts nine clergy running for federal office this cycle as Democrats — something he hasn’t seen before. “The idea that a faith leader, especially a white faith leader, would run as a Democrat and be forthright about it … it's really unusual,” Pagitt said. “We've had candidates [in the past] whose moms were pastors, and they were nervous about mentioning that in the Democratic Party circles. But that seems to have shifted and changed.”

Además, el Gobierno ofrece su versión del contenido una a una de las nueve comunicaciones efectivas, también para desmentir a Vivas y su idea de que Ceuta alertó de lo que venía pero en La Moncloa no le hicieron caso.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/el-gobierno-desvela-las-conversaciones-con-ceuta-para-desmentir-a-vivas.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/el-presidente-de-ceuta-acude-a-la-audiencia-nacional-para-declarar-como-testigo-por-la-entrada-masiva-de-julio.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/el-presidente-de-ceuta-acude-a-la-audiencia-nacional-para-declarar-como-testigo-por-la-entrada-masiva-de-julio.html">Durante más de dos horas y media, el presidente de Ceuta</a> desgranó en la Audiencia Nacional las llamadas, mensajes o intentos de contactos que desde la ciudad se mantuvieron con el Gobierno durante los últimos días de julio, cuando la situación migratoria se estaba desbordando, antes de la entrada de entre 70.000 y 80.000 personas desde Marruecos. En total, entre los días 27, 28 y 29, Juan Jesús Vivas aseguró que se produjeron nueve llamadas al jefe de gabinete de Pedro Sánchez (más una el propio día 30) y que habló personalmente con tres ministros: el de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres; el de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares; y la de Defensa, Margarita Robles. Además, relató que también intentó hablar con el responsable de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, con cuya secretaria de Estado sí estuvo en contacto permanente esos días con la intención de transmitir que la situación migratoria de la ciudad ya entonces era extraordinaria y que era necesario tomar medidas como un refuerzo policial o la creación del mando único. El día 30, con la frontera ya descontrolada, volvió a llamar al jefe de gabinete de Sánchez, Diego Rubio, y logró hablar tanto con Marlaska como con Sánchez.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/los-tres-dias-previos-a-la-entrada-masiva-en-ceuta-segun-el-relato-de-vivas-ante-la-jueza.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Los tres días previos a la entrada masiva en Ceuta, según el relato de Vivas ante la jueza

articles.body: <p>13 y 14 de octubre. Esos serán los días en los que el rey Felipe VI y Letizia Ortiz visiten Ceuta y Melilla, según han informado este jueves fuentes de la Casa del Rey y de La Moncloa. Viaje al que no les acompañará el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, según han adelantado desde el Ejecutivo a la agencia Efe y ha confirmado este periódico. Las fechas se habían convertido en el secreto de Estado mejor guardado de los últimos tiempos. Después de dos meses de elucubraciones, expectativas y rifirrafes entre el Gobierno de Ceuta, el Ejecutivo central y Zarzuela, el calendario queda por fin despejado, además, antes de que todos los mandatarios civiles y militares coincidan, con motivo de los fastos de la fiesta nacional, el próximo 12 de octubre. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/los-reyes-visitaran-ceuta-y-melilla-los-dias-13-y-14-de-octubre.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

"></img><p>De <a href="https://elpais.com/opinion/2023-03-06/el-pisito.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/opinion/2023-03-06/el-pisito.html"><i>El pisito, </i>de Rafael Azcona,</a> donde un joven se casa con una anciana para así heredar el piso de ella y poderse algún día instalar allí con su novia, hasta <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-09-23/maricarmen-se-queda-un-centenar-de-activistas-espera-junto-a-la-anciana-a-la-comision-judicial.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-09-23/maricarmen-se-queda-un-centenar-de-activistas-espera-junto-a-la-anciana-a-la-comision-judicial.html">el desahucio de Maricarmen</a>, perpetrado la semana pasada, se condensa la historia inmobiliaria de Madrid como género literario. Esta fue la aventura de nuestros padres y será la aventura de nuestros hijos: sobrevivir con dignidad a un entorno social áspero y desalmado. Las grandes ciudades son máquinas de fabricar soledades acompañadas. La otra mañana, la falta de imaginación moral de las sentencias de la Audiencia Provincial y del Supremo <a href="https://elpais.com/opinion/2026-09-23/el-simbolo-de-un-derecho-roto.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/opinion/2026-09-23/el-simbolo-de-un-derecho-roto.html">permitió arrancar de su casa</a> a una mujer de 87 años y sacarla de allí en camilla tras toda una vida entre esas paredes. Hizo falta sumar varias dotaciones de antidisturbios, equipo médico de urgencia, helicópteros y <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-09-25/tirones-de-cuello-porrazos-y-aranazos-las-agresiones-policiales-del-desahucio-de-maricarmen-que-investigara-delegacion-de-gobierno.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-09-25/tirones-de-cuello-porrazos-y-aranazos-las-agresiones-policiales-del-desahucio-de-maricarmen-que-investigara-delegacion-de-gobierno.html">brutales cargas contra la resistencia civil</a> como si se afrontara la amenaza de un comando terrorista. El terrorismo inmobiliario tiene de su parte a la ley, mientras no se racionalice la legislación. La precariedad histórica en los últimos años ha aumentado con la venta de pisos de protección oficial <a href="https://elpais.com/economia/2026-09-28/las-leyes-que-dieron-alas-a-los-buitres.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/economia/2026-09-28/las-leyes-que-dieron-alas-a-los-buitres.html">a los fondos de capital</a> y la festiva llegada de las grandes fortunas que, con el dinero extraído de sus naciones empobrecidas, compran a precios desorbitados los mejores espacios de la capital. A esto lo llamamos éxito. Imagínense lo que será el fracaso.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/opinion/2026-09-29/terror-inmobiliario.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Terror inmobiliario

articles.body: <img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/H6ETR6DFKBCKBKEK5AGQBQW3O4.jpg?auth=eadf10c8843292a528c4ae2aa499604784373c2e12979946cf8cbd2bda60c766" width="8192" height="5464" alt="La acampada de Sol, este lunes. "></img><p>Ana Orantes Ruiz <a href="https://elpais.com/sociedad/2022-12-17/25-anos-del-asesinato-de-ana-orantes-que-cambio-la-lucha-contra-la-violencia-machista-en-espana.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/sociedad/2022-12-17/25-anos-del-asesinato-de-ana-orantes-que-cambio-la-lucha-contra-la-violencia-machista-en-espana.html">murió asesinada por su exmarido</a> el 17 de diciembre de 1997. Dos semanas antes, había aparecido en un programa de Canal Sur contando 40 años de palizas. Se había divorciado, pero el juez determinó que ella y su marido siguieran en su casa de Cúllar Vega (Granada). Ella arriba, él abajo, compartiendo el patio. Él pasaba poco por allí, pero a veces volvía. La última, después de verla en la tele. <a href="https://elpais.com/diario/1997/12/18/espana/882399613_850215.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/diario/1997/12/18/espana/882399613_850215.html">La quemó viva en aquel patio compartido.</a> Fue una más de las mujeres maltratadas por sus parejas. De las mujeres asesinadas. Pero su historia conmocionó a la sociedad y <a href="https://elpais.com/politica/2017/11/24/actualidad/1511548723_149638.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/politica/2017/11/24/actualidad/1511548723_149638.html">convirtió en público un problema</a> que hasta entonces se consideraba privado. Este crimen cambió la sensibilidad de la sociedad e impulsó cambios legislativos para afrontarla. En 1999, el Gobierno de Aznar modificó el Código Penal. La violencia psicológica se convirtió en delito y aparecieron las órdenes de alejamiento. En 2004, el Gobierno de Zapatero aprobó <a href="https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-21760" target="_self" rel="" title="https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-21760">la ley integral contra la violencia de género</a> y en 2007, <a href="https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-6115" target="_self" rel="" title="https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-6115">la Ley para la Igualdad Efectiva de Mujeres y Hombres.</a> El crimen de Ana Orantes despertó la conciencia colectiva ante un problema social que ya existía. Y ese despertar cambió un marco legal que hasta entonces no contemplaba respuestas.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/opinion/2026-09-29/maricarmen-una-mas-de-las-que-impulsaron-un-cambio.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>Podemos ha confirmado este jueves lo que en las últimas horas parecía ya un secreto a voces, que sus cuatro diputados apoyarán mañana en el Congreso los dos decretos del Gobierno sobre vivienda. Su respaldo deja ahora la aprobación de ambas normas en manos de Junts, que ha expresado algunas reticencias, a pesar de que el Ejecutivo, el miércoles, se mostraba “optimista”. La formación de Ione Belarra, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/los-socios-de-izquierda-presionan-a-podemos-para-que-permita-los-decretos-de-vivienda-como-punto-de-partida.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/los-socios-de-izquierda-presionan-a-podemos-para-que-permita-los-decretos-de-vivienda-como-punto-de-partida.html">que se había manifestado muy crítica con el Gobierno por plantear dos textos separados</a> (uno solo para prorrogar de manera indefinida los alquileres), ha anunciado su decisión <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/el-apoyo-del-sindicato-de-inquilinas-a-los-dos-decretos-de-vivienda-eleva-la-presion-sobre-podemos.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/el-apoyo-del-sindicato-de-inquilinas-a-los-dos-decretos-de-vivienda-eleva-la-presion-sobre-podemos.html">tras reunirse con la Confederación de Sindicatos de Inquilinas esta mañana.</a> El colectivo ya llamó ayer a los grupos a votar a favor de los dos paquetes legislativos. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/podemos-anuncia-su-apoyo-a-los-decretos-de-vivienda-en-el-congreso.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/el-gobierno-desvela-las-conversaciones-con-ceuta-para-desmentir-a-vivas.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/el-gobierno-desvela-las-conversaciones-con-ceuta-para-desmentir-a-vivas.html">El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska</a>, se ha visto en persona con sus colegas de la UE por primera vez tras la crisis migratoria en Ceuta. Ahí, en el consejo de Interior que se celebra este jueves en Luxemburgo, ha defendido la “solidaridad operativa, financiera y política” ante el resto de responsables de la cartera en una intervención sobre el estado del área Schengen, según el departamento que dirige. Esas palabras suenan a reproche tras la reacción que hubo en los primeros días de agosto, después de la entrada masiva de migrantes en la frontera de la ciudad autónoma con Marruecos, cuando 22 Estados miembros firmaron una carta muy dura con España y la política migratoria del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/marlaska-exige-solidaridad-financiera-y-politica-a-la-ue-ante-crisis-migratorias-como-la-de-ceuta.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Marlaska exige “solidaridad financiera y política” a la UE ante crisis migratorias como la de Ceuta

articles.body: <p>La Guardia Civil ha detenido a cinco personas, dos de ellas menores de edad, por su presunta relación con una agresión racista denunciada en Tavernes de la Valldigna (Valencia) que tuvo lugar la madrugada de un domingo mientras se celebraban las fiestas en el municipio. articles.body: <p>El presidente del Tribunal Constitucional (TC), Cándido Conde-Pumpido, ha hecho un llamamiento este jueves a las fuerzas políticas para que se pongan de acuerdo en el Senado con la <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2025-12-12/el-pp-bloquea-la-renovacion-del-tribunal-constitucional-por-el-clima-politico-el-gobierno-esta-saltando-por-los-aires.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2025-12-12/el-pp-bloquea-la-renovacion-del-tribunal-constitucional-por-el-clima-politico-el-gobierno-esta-saltando-por-los-aires.html">renovación de los miembros del tribunal</a>, cuyo mandato acabó en diciembre de 2025 (entre los que se encuentra él mismo). El magistrado ha instado a las fuerzas políticas a que cumplan con el mandato que les impone la carta magna: “No puede haber otros intereses políticos de cualquier otra naturaleza que se superpongan al cumplimiento de la Constitución Española”. En ese sentido, el magistrado ha recordado que el texto constitucional “dice claramente” que los miembros del tribunal de garantías “serán designados por un periodo de nueve años”. Y ha insistido en que dicho periodo “ya ha transcurrido”.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/el-presidente-del-constitucional-insta-a-los-partidos-a-que-cumplan-con-su-obligacion-en-el-senado-y-renueven-el-tribunal.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: El presidente del Constitucional insta a los partidos a que cumplan con su obligación en el Senado y renueven el tribunal

articles.body: <p>Cada mañana, nuevos jóvenes aparecen con golpes caminando por las calles de Ceuta: una brecha en la cabeza, un tobillo hinchado, un brazo dislocado, el costado amoratado, una raja de lado a lado de la cara. Y siempre es la misma explicación: me pegaron los soldados. Decenas de testimonios recogidos en distintos puntos de Ceuta entre jóvenes sin relación entre sí, con el único vínculo de dormir cada día a la intemperie en la ciudad autónoma, coinciden al describir las palizas que sufren cada noche a manos del Ejército. Parejas de soldados que irrumpen por la noche entre los cañaverales, las arboledas o las rocas de la playa para aplicar una metodología violenta que comenzó con la llegada masiva de decenas de miles de migrantes hace dos meses. Este martes, Amnistía Internacional recogió <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/amnistia-internacional-denuncia-tortura-y-malos-tratos-a-los-inmigrantes-en-ceuta.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/amnistia-internacional-denuncia-tortura-y-malos-tratos-a-los-inmigrantes-en-ceuta.html">en un informe una veintena de casos </a>y los envió a los presidentes del Gobierno español, Pedro Sánchez, y de la ciudad de Ceuta, <a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/juan-jesus-vivas-lara/" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/juan-jesus-vivas-lara/">Juan Jesús Vivas</a>. Pero los testimonios recogidos por AI no son los únicos. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/decenas-de-migrantes-denuncian-agresiones-de-militares-nos-dicen-que-si-no-nos-vamos-seguiran-las-palizas.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Decenas de migrantes denuncian agresiones de militares: “Nos dicen que si no nos vamos, seguirán las palizas”

articles.body: <p>El Centro de Coordinación de Emergencias de la Generalitat Valenciana ha lanzado pasados unos minutos de las diez de la mañana un mensaje masivo <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/comunidad-valenciana/2026-09-16/la-generalitat-envia-un-es-alert-por-el-riesgo-de-inundaciones-y-activa-la-preemergencia-hidrologica-tras-las-fuertes-lluvias-en-valencia.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/comunidad-valenciana/2026-09-16/la-generalitat-envia-un-es-alert-por-el-riesgo-de-inundaciones-y-activa-la-preemergencia-hidrologica-tras-las-fuertes-lluvias-en-valencia.html">ES-Alert </a>por el peligro extraordinario de lluvias torrenciales, sobre todo, a partir de las seis de la tarde de este jueves en las provincias de Castellón y Valencia. articles.body: <p>La madrugada del 1 de octubre de 2023, un devastador incendio <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2023-10-01/tragedia-en-las-discotecas-de-atalayas-el-principal-poligono-del-ocio-nocturno-de-murcia.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2023-10-01/tragedia-en-las-discotecas-de-atalayas-el-principal-poligono-del-ocio-nocturno-de-murcia.html">arrasó las discotecas Teatre y Fonda Milagros</a>, en la zona de ocio de Murcia conocida como Atalayas. Trece personas fallecieron y, después de tres años de investigación, el pasado mes de julio la jueza solicitó la apertura de juicio oral para los cuatro responsables de las discotecas, además de un DJ, el propietario de una máquina de fuegos fríos que supuestamente originó el incendio y el ingeniero que dividió en dos la nave que ocupaban las dos salas. Las familias de las víctimas <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-09/siete-personas-se-sentaran-en-el-banquillo-por-el-incendio-en-las-discotecas-de-murcia-en-el-que-fallecieron-13-personas.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-09/siete-personas-se-sentaran-en-el-banquillo-por-el-incendio-en-las-discotecas-de-murcia-en-el-que-fallecieron-13-personas.html">aguardan que se fije la fecha del juicio</a> entre el dolor, la esperanza de que se haga justicia, la frustración de que no se vaya a investigar a ningún representante del Ayuntamiento de Murcia y el sentimiento de abandono por parte de las administraciones. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-01/tres-anos-despues-del-incendio-de-las-discotecas-en-murcia-nunca-tuvimos-ayuda-moral-o-economica-ahora-solo-esperamos-tener-justicia.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Tres años después del incendio de las discotecas en Murcia: “Nunca tuvimos ayuda moral o económica. Ahora solo esperamos tener justicia”

articles.body: <p>El acuerdo político por la vivienda permanece aguardando en el rellano. Junts per Catalunya ha avanzado que <a href="https://elpais.com/economia/vivienda/2026-09-29/las-claves-de-los-decretos-de-vivienda-frenazo-a-los-desahucios-y-castigos-a-los-fondos-buitre.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/economia/vivienda/2026-09-29/las-claves-de-los-decretos-de-vivienda-frenazo-a-los-desahucios-y-castigos-a-los-fondos-buitre.html">no le convence el contenido</a> de los dos reales decretos aprobados el martes por el Consejo de Ministros. Su voto en contra no es definitivo, pero la negociación se ha enmarañado. Junts alega que, con el redactado actual, no se veta la compra de pisos a los fondos buitres ―“clarísimamente no”, dicen desde el partido independentista― y además se pisa una gruesa línea roja para los postulados de la formación: los pequeños propietarios quedan desprotegidos. El resultado es que siguen <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/los-socios-de-izquierda-presionan-a-podemos-para-que-permita-los-decretos-de-vivienda-como-punto-de-partida.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-30/los-socios-de-izquierda-presionan-a-podemos-para-que-permita-los-decretos-de-vivienda-como-punto-de-partida.html">sin estar asegurados los apoyos</a> suficientes para ratificar en el Congreso este viernes los decretos que supuestamente deben corregir anomalías en un mercado inmobiliario de precios disparados y, de paso, ayudar a rebajar la ola de indignación ciudadana que ha propiciado <a href="https://elpais.com/opinion/2026-09-29/maricarmen-una-mas-de-las-que-impulsaron-un-cambio.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/opinion/2026-09-29/maricarmen-una-mas-de-las-que-impulsaron-un-cambio.html">el caso de Maricarmen Abascal</a>. Junts asegura sentir “decepción” y guarda distancias con el Gobierno, ante una votación cuatro días antes de que la ley de amnistía tenga la luz verde definitiva y abra la puerta al regreso de Carles Puigdemont.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-01/junts-entre-dos-fuegos-aceptar-la-regulacion-del-mercado-de-la-vivienda-o-el-portazo-a-sanchez-a-cuatro-dias-de-la-amnistia.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

"></img><p>Si necesitas agua o comida. Si no sabes dónde colocar la esterilla. Si quieres enterarte de las actividades del día. Si te ha llegado un burofax y tienes que dejar tu piso. Si te han subido un 50% el alquiler. Sea lo que sea, tienes que preguntar a los chicos y chicas que van de naranja, antes con camisetas, ahora cada vez más chalecos. Es el color insignia del Sindicato de Inquilinas, la asociación que <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-09-29/de-sol-no-se-mueve-nadie.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-09-29/de-sol-no-se-mueve-nadie.html">lidera la multitudinaria acampada</a> ―miles de personas durmiendo en cientos de tiendas― en la Puerta del Sol. Con esa misma frase, hace nueve años, un puñado de personas se reunió en dos pequeños locales de Madrid y Barcelona para presentar la plataforma que hoy encabeza <a href="https://elpais.com/economia/vivienda/2026-09-30/el-casero-tendra-que-indemnizar-con-12-mensualidades-al-inquilino-si-decide-no-renovar-el-alquiler.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/economia/vivienda/2026-09-30/el-casero-tendra-que-indemnizar-con-12-mensualidades-al-inquilino-si-decide-no-renovar-el-alquiler.html">la lucha por el derecho a la vivienda</a> en España. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-10-01/quienes-son-los-de-los-chalecos-naranjas-asi-funciona-el-sindicato-de-inquilinas-que-lidera-la-acampada-de-sol.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: L’Ajuntament de Barcelona ha activat en fase d’alerta el Pla d’actuació d’emergència municipal per risc d’insuficiència drenant davant la previsió de les pluges intenses i tempestes previstes per a aquest dijous a la ciutat. Només 24 hores després de desactivar aquest pla pels aiguats que van descarregar a la ciutat dimarts , el consistori torna a demanar prudència a la ciutadania. En aquest sentit, es recomana revisar els desguassos i baixants i desconnectar aparells elèctrics. En el cas dels conductors, es recorda que s’ha de moderar la velocitat i ampliar la distància de seguretat amb la resta de vehicles. També et pot interessar L’Inuncat, en alerta una altra vegada per la previsió de pluja torrencial dijous a Catalunya Manel Cascante Torrella 3 minuts de lectura En alerta també el pla Inuncat Protecció Civil també ha activat en fase d’alerta el pla Inuncat i el Meteocat ha emès avisos d’intensitat de precipitació, amb un llindar màxim de 40 litres en 30 minuts. L‘ avís afecta bona part de Catalunya , inclosos el litoral i prelitoral centrals, durant el matí de dijous (de 8 a 14 h). Es tracta d’un avís de perill de grau alt, 4 sobre una escala de 6, és a dir, indica que hi ha entre un 30 i un 70 % de probabilitat que caiguin més de 40 litres en 30 minuts. articles.body: (ACN) L’activista Roger Español afronta l’últim dia del seu judici a l’ Audiència de Barcelona convençut de la culpabilitat dels policies acusats de buidar-li un ull. En una atenció a mitjans al passeig de Lluís Companys de la capital catalana, ha dit que tenen totes les proves pericials que els donen la raó sobre la “ brutalitat policial ” als manifestants l’1-O. A més, creu que el procés és part d’una lluita “per acabar amb les pilotes de goma “. El final del judici coincideix amb el novè aniversari del referèndum , i desenes d’independentistes s’han concentrat davant l’Audiència per donar suport a Español i per marcar l’efemèride, amb pancartes recordant els 1.066 ferits de l’1-O i les escoles on la policia va carregar contra votants i manifestants. També et pot interessar Els Mossos descarten que l’escopeter acusat de buidar l’ull a Roger Español l’apuntés directament Francis Manzano Rojas 3 minuts de lectura Español reivindica “fer memòria” A les portes del tribunal, Español ha dit que el judici no només busca la condemna dels policies, sinó continuar la lluita “contra la impunitat policial , especialment quan hi ha moviments independentistes implicats”. Aprofitant l’aniversari de l’1-O, també ha reivindicat “el camí” que el sobiranisme va fer aquell dia i “fer memòria” de la resposta de l’Estat . L’advocada d ‘Irídia , Anaïs Franquesa, ha dit que al judici “s’ha demostrat” que un escopeter va disparar tres vegades en direcció a Roger Español i que sabia que les armes que empren “són potencialment letals”. Segons ella, li va disparar “amb ànim de castigar-lo per la conducta que havia tingut anteriorment” i ha quedat demostrat que els acusats “es van saltar la normativa totalment amb la intenció de lesionar”. També et pot interessar Comença el judici contra els policies que van mutilar Roger Español en les càrregues de l’1-O Marina Sancho Núria Granados 4 minuts de lectura L’activista Carles Guillot, de Stop Bales de Goma , ha dit que una vintena de persones han mort a l’estat com a conseqüència de l’impacte d’una bala de goma i una quarantena han acabat mutilats i mai hi ha hagut cap policia condemnat. Les entitats esperen la culpabilitat dels acusats El president d’ Òmnium , Xavier Antich, ha dit que la “violència i repressió” de les forces policials espanyoles van ser “impròpies d’un estat democràtic” i l’entitat espera la culpabilitat dels agents acusats. En la mateixa línia, el president de l’ ANC , Josep Vila, creu que els quatre acusats van exercir “violència premeditada” contra ciutadans pacífics. Vila, així com Antich, ha recordat l’1-O, i ha dit que ni la finalització del judici ni l’amnistia aturarà la causa independentista. “ Continuarem plantant cara “, ha afirmat. També et pot interessar Campanya de suport a Roger Español pel judici contra els policies que li van disparar a l’ull l’1-O Redacció 5 minuts de lectura Ajornada la sessió fins al migdia La sessió d’aquest dijous ha quedat suspesa després que un dels acusats no hagi comparegut per motius de salut. Segons ha explicat la representant de l’advocacia de l’Estat que exerceix de defensa del policia, es tracta de l’inspector del cos de la Policia Nacional acusat. “Ha concorregut en una causa mèdica sobtada i sobrevinguda que l’impedeix comparèixer”, ha explicat. El tribunal ha decidit ajornar la sessió fins a les 13 hores . Benet Salellas, l’advocat d’Español, ha exigit que es dicti una ordre de recerca i captura contra aquest policia.
articles.headline: Roger Español afronta l’últim dia de judici reclamant la culpabilitat dels policies

articles.body: (ACN/Redacció) El servei de tramvia de les línies T1, T2 i T3 no cobrirà el recorregut entre Francesc Macià i Montesa els dies 10, 11 i 12 d’octubr e per unes obres de renovació de la via previstes en aquest tram de la xarxa del Trambaix. Així, des de les 5 del matí del dissabte 10 fins a la finalització del servei del dilluns 12, aquestes tres línies només oferiran servei entre les seves terminals (Bon Viatge, Llevant-Les Planes i Sant Feliu | Comarcal), i la parada de Montesa. Per cobrir el tram suspès, hi haurà un servei alternatiu en bus . Les obres també afectaran la circulació viària al tram lateral de la Diagonal, tallada a l’altura de doctor Marañón i fins a John Maynard Keynes. També et pot interessar El TRAM torna a circular a Glòries després d’un estiu de talls per les obres a la Gran Via Pablo Mena 2 minuts de lectura Les obres han de permetre renovar completament el carril de les dues vies al voltant del carrer d’Adolf Florensa, una actuació preventiva que permetrà mantenir els estàndards de seguretat i fiabilitat de la infraestructura abans que els elements actuals arribin al final de la seva vida útil. Està previst que el dimarts 13 d’octubre el servei es reprengui amb normalitat a les 5 h del matí, tot i que continuaran les afectacions al trànsit dins la mitjanit del mateix dia.

articles.body: (ACN) Un total de 95 persones han mort en 91 accidents mortals a la xarxa viària interurbana de Catalunya fins al setembre, segons dades provisionals del Servei Català de Trànsit. La xifra representa un 16 % menys que en el mateix període de l’any passa t, en què van ser 113 víctimes mortals en 105 sinistres. En comparació amb el 2019, que és l’any de referència per al compliment d’objectius de reducció, s’han registrat 41 víctimes mortals menys, fet que representa una reducció del 30 %. Dels 95 morts, 77 eren homes i 18 dones. Al setembre s’han produït 10 morts, mentre que l’any passat en van ser 15. D’altra banda, s’han registrat 561 ferits greus , un 15 % menys que els 661 del mateix període del 2025. Gairebé un 57 % de les víctimes mortals eren vulnerables —54 de 95. En total, 36 eren motoristes , dos menys que l’any passat. Enguany, aquest és el col·lectiu del conjunt d’usuaris que registra més morts. A més, hi ha hagut nou vianants morts i nou ciclistes. També et pot interessar Els motoristes morts en accident de trànsit a Barcelona ja superen la xifra del 2025 Marta Casals Torres 2 minuts de lectura Baixen les mortes a Barcelona, Tarragona i Lleida i pugen a Girona Per demarcacions, Barcelona concentra 38 de les 95 víctimes mortals, tot i que registra una reducció del 25,5 % respecte de l’any passat. El Baix Llobregat és la comarca amb més morts, amb nou. A la demarcació de Tarragona hi ha hagut 20 víctimes mortals, quatre menys que en el mateix període del 2025, la qual cosa suposa un descens del 17 %. Comparat amb el 2019, aquest decreixement arriba al 40 %. A més, no hi ha hagut cap víctima mortal a l’AP-7 en el tram de Tarragona , mentre el 2019 i durant el mateix període n’hi va haver set i l’any passat, onze. Girona ha registrat 23 víctimes mortals aquests primers nou mesos, set més que l’any anterior. La Selva és la comarca amb més víctimes, amb vuit. Pel que fa a Lleida, s’han registrat 14 morts, vuit menys que el 2025.
